newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S peace moves delayed by Jerusalem bombings.
newsitem.headline: U.S peace moves delayed by Jerusalem bombings.

text.p: Two Arab suicide bombers killed 12 people in a crowded Jerusalem market on Wednesday, setting back fresh U.S. efforts to resolve an Israel-PLO peace crisis that has now deepened.

Israeli police said the bombers, wearing jackets and ties, strolled into crowds of lunchtime shoppers at the Mahane Yehuda market in west Jerusalem with 10-kg (22-pound) bombs concealed in attache cases and blew themselves up.

"The slaughter was aimed directly at innocent Israelis, and make no mistake, it was also aimed at the majority of Israelis, Palestinians and Arabs who want a lasting and just peace," U.S. President Bill Clinton told reporters at the White House.
World leaders and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the bombing, the deadliest attack against Israelis since March 1996.

Clinton said a visit to the region by U.S. mediator Dennis Ross, who had been expected to present new ideas on ending a peacemaking deadlock over Israeli settlement building, was being postponed to allow a period of mourning in the Jewish state.
Ross had been scheduled to arrive in the region on Thursday.

The Islamic militant movement Hamas claimed responsibility for the attack in a leaflet faxed to an international news agency. Hamas gave Israel until 1800 GMT on Sunday to free all Palestinian prisoners including its founder Sheikh Ahmed Yassin. It did not elaborate.

Hamas sources said the group's Izz el-Din al-Qassam military brigades carried out the attack in Jerusalem's main Jewish market to avenge a Jewish woman's pasting of posters on Hebron storefronts depicting the Moslem Prophet Mohammad as a pig.

They said it also was in retaliation for the publication in an Israeli science magazine of a photomontage of the Virgin Mary with a cow's head. The photo, to illustrate a story on cloning, angered Palestinian Christians.
Israel clamped a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded Arafat crack down on Moslem militants.

"We expect the Palestinian Authority and its leader to begin to fight terror as they are committed to, as they haven't done until today, that they will take all the steps required against these terrorists and their operators who roam free," he told a news conference after visiting wounded in hospital.
Arafat called Netanyahu to express his condolences, but the Israeli leader, in a "very tough conversation" replied that voicing sorrow was not enough, the prime minister's spokesman said.
"I condemn completely this terrorist act because it is against the peace process, against the Palestinians, and against the Israelis," Arafat told Reuters hours later.
A senior PLO security official said Arafat had declared a state of emergency in all Palestinian areas and ordered the arrest of activists of "extremist groups" including Hamas and Islamic Jihad.
"The arrests have already started," the official said.
In a statement, Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Wallis said Pope John Paul condemned the bombing and stressed that violence only breeds fresh violence.
"Peace, however, is made through continued dialogue and respect for promises already undertaken," the statement said.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who visited Syria and Jordan on Tuesday as part of Cairo's bid to jump start Middle East peace efforts, called Netanyahu to offer his sympathy, Israeli and Egyptian spokesmen said.
In Cairo, Foreign Minister Amr Moussa urged all sides "to keep the peace" and said "what is important in moments like these is confirmation that the peace process will continue".
The European Union, which also has been mediating between Israel and the Palestinians, strongly condemned the attack and urged Israelis not to let it derail the peace process.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan called the bombings "abominable and unfortunate" and appealed to both sides to return to the negotiating table.

Annan recalled telling Netanyahu in a telephone conversation on Monday that he was encouraged by his suspension of construction of a controversial housing project in an Arab neighbourhood in East Jerusalem.
"And so I am disappointed that at a crucial time when we were just on the verge of getting the talks back on track that this should happen," Annan said.

It was Netanyahu's decision in March to plough ahead with another project, the construction of a 6,500-home Jewish settlement on the outskirts of Arab East Jerusalem, that plunged peacemaking into crisis.
France, Britain and Germany coupled their condemnations of the bombings with appeals to keep peace hopes alive.
"Only the resumption of the peace process, which is necessary and urgent, can open the way to a future for all peoples of the region," French President Jacques Chirac said in a letter to Netanyahu.
